title: Gradient descent on a bowl
summary: Gradient descent by hand, starting from least squares: the gradient, one step downhill, how the step size (learning rate) decides converge or diverge, the eigenvalues and condition number of a bowl, and least squares solved by walking downhill.
written: Written by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 16 Nov 2026, after the least-squares and PCA courses and docs/seed-context.md. Every example designed in sympy first so each hand computation is an integer or a simple fraction. Every answer key is re-derived with sympy by tools/validate_courses.py.

sources.name: Mark's notes and chats (seed context)
sources.note: docs/seed-context.md: least squares and the normal equations already his, optimisation listed as a gap, he compares guesses before optimising, and his slips (signs, a factor not applied to every term).

sources.name: Gradient descent (Wikipedia)
sources.note: The update x_{n+1} = x_n − η∇f(x_n) with η called the step size or learning rate; the negative gradient as the direction of fastest decrease; the gradient of ‖Ax − b‖² as 2Aᵀ(Ax − b) (so Aᵀ(Ax − b) for this course's ½‖Ax − b‖²); iteration counts growing with the condition number of AᵀA and the zig-zag path when it is large.

sources.name: Gabriel Goh, Why Momentum Really Works (Distill, 2017)
sources.note: The eigenvalue view of gradient descent on ½wᵀAw − bᵀw: each eigen-component multiplied by (1 − αλᵢ) per step, convergence exactly when 0 < αλᵢ < 2 for every i, the best fixed step 2/(λ_min + λ_max) with rate (κ − 1)/(κ + 1), and κ = λ_max/λ_min. This course writes η for Goh's α.

sources.name: Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Cambridge, 2004), section 9.3
sources.note: Algorithm 9.3 (step along −∇f, then update) and the example f = ½(x₁² + γx₂²), whose Hessian has eigenvalues 1 and γ and whose sublevel sets have condition number max(γ, 1/γ). Read in the free PDF linked from the book's page.

sources.name: Gilbert Strang, MIT 18.065 (Spring 2018), Lecture 22: Gradient Descent: Downhill to a Minimum
sources.note: From the lecture page's summary: the step x − s∇F, and the example F = ½(x² + by²), whose path zig-zags towards (0, 0) when b is small.

sources.name: MIT 18.065 (Spring 2018), Lecture 25: Stochastic Gradient Descent (Suvrit Sra)
sources.note: From the lecture page's summary: stochastic gradient descent uses a random minibatch per step instead of all the data, and is the main method for training large machine-learning models. Used only for the last screen's two sentences.

lessons.title: A landscape and its gradient
lessons.summary: Heights on x² + 2y², both partial derivatives, and the gradient pointing uphill.

lessons.title: One step downhill
lessons.summary: x_{k+1} = x_k − η∇f(x_k) by hand, twice, with f falling each time.

lessons.title: How big a step
lessons.summary: On ½λx² each step multiplies x by 1 − ηλ, so it converges exactly when 0 < η < 2/λ.

lessons.title: Two directions at once
lessons.summary: The largest eigenvalue caps η, the smallest sets the crawl, and κ = λmax/λmin measures the zig-zag.

lessons.title: Least squares by walking downhill
lessons.summary: ∇½‖Ax − b‖² = Aᵀ(Ax − b): zero gradient is the normal equations, and AᵀA sets the step size.
